terms.comment: Properly a loud noise, an outcry (of a crowd, of frogs, of cicadas); then, most often, loud abuse. Cicero: an insult thrown petulantius, rudely, is a convīcium (Cael. 6). Convīcium facere alicui, to shout abuse at someone.
A word said against someone; the verb is maledīcere with the dative (Cic. Deiot. 28), which Cicero distinguishes from a formal accusation (Cael. 6).

terms.grammar: phrase, also written as one word, maledīcō, maledīcere, maledīxī, maledictum
evidence: Plaut. Bacch. 1.2.10: quī bonīs dīcunt male (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: saepe manū summā lacrimantia lūmina terget immeritōque furēns dīcit convīcia fūmō
phrases.english: often he wipes his streaming eyes with the back of his hand, and in a rage swears at the blameless smoke
explain an insult and you make it sharper

sources: Lewis & Short: convicium · Lewis & Short: maledictum · Lewis & Short: maledico
